chapters.title: Chapter 3: What Your ESOPs Are Really Worth

lessons.title: Reading Your Grant Letter: The Questions to Ask Before You Accept

children.text: By now you know what the words mean. This lesson is about the document itself: what you should receive, which clauses decide your outcome, what good looks like, and what to say when something is missing. Read this before you accept your next grant, and reread it the week you resign.

body.text: A grant letter is a contract you will live with for years and probably read for ninety seconds. Ten focused minutes, before you sign, is the highest return work you will ever do on your ESOPs.

children.text: Collect Three Documents, Not One
Most employees receive only a
grant letter
and assume that is the deal. It is not. The letter sits underneath the
scheme document
, which is where the terms that actually hurt tend to live.

markDefs.definition: The individual letter recording your specific grant: quantity, exercise price, vesting schedule and dates.
The master document, approved by shareholders, that governs the whole ESOP plan. Your grant letter sits under it and cannot override it.

body.title: Ask HR for All of These, in Writing
steps: The ESOP scheme or plan document approved by shareholders
Your individual grant letter, signed and dated
Confirmation of the board or committee resolution approving your grant
The current fully diluted share count, and the date it was measured
The latest fair market value per share, and the valuation date
Any amendment to the scheme made since it was first approved

body.text: If a company will not share the scheme document with a prospective or current employee, treat that as information in itself. You are being asked to accept a contract whose terms you are not allowed to read.

children.text: The Eight Clauses That Decide Your Outcome

body.caption: What to look for, and what should worry you

cells: Quantity and denominator
Options stated with the fully diluted share count, so you can compute a percentage
A number of options with no share count disclosed
Exercise price
Fixed, stated in rupees, at or near face value for an early-stage company
A price to be determined later, or tied to a future valuation
Vesting schedule
Four years, one-year cliff, monthly or quarterly after that
Heavily back-loaded, or vesting entirely at the end
Exercise window on exit
Several years, or until a liquidity event
30 to 90 days at an unlisted company with no buyback history
Leaver definitions
Clear, narrow definition of cause, tied to defined misconduct
Cause defined broadly, or determined at the board’s sole discretion
Clawback
Limited to fraud or serious misconduct
Repurchase of vested shares at face value in wide circumstances
Change of control
Double trigger acceleration, stated explicitly
Silence, or a clause letting the board cancel options on a deal
Amendment rights
Changes that hurt existing grants need your consent
The company may amend the scheme at any time, at its discretion

children.text: Two words deserve special attention wherever they appear:
discretion
and
clawback
. Both convert your entitlement into somebody else’s decision.

markDefs.definition: A clause letting the board or a committee decide something on its own judgement, with no obligation to you.
A provision allowing the company to cancel options or repurchase shares, often at a nominal price, in defined circumstances.

children.text: Decode a Real-Looking Letter
Here is a clause of the kind you will actually meet.

"The Company hereby grants you 8,000 Options under the Employee Stock Option Scheme, at an Exercise Price of ₹25 per Option. Options shall vest over four years, with 25% vesting on the first anniversary of the Grant Date and the balance vesting in equal quarterly instalments thereafter. Vested Options must be exercised within 60 days of the Cessation Date, failing which they shall lapse. The Board may, at its sole discretion, amend, suspend or terminate the Scheme at any time."
What it tells you
The grant size is clear, but useless on its own. With 40,00,000 fully diluted shares, 8,000 options is 0.2% of the company.
At a fair market value of ₹250 a share, that is ₹20,00,000 gross, or ₹18,00,000 after the ₹25 exercise price, at today’s valuation and before tax.
The vesting is standard and reasonable: a one-year cliff of 2,000 options, then 500 a quarter.
The 60-day exercise window is the clause that can destroy the value. You would need ₹2,00,000 plus perquisite tax within two months of leaving.
The amendment clause is unlimited on its face. Ask whether changes adverse to existing grants require consent.

body.title: Convert Options into Ownership
body.prompt: The letter grants 8,000 options and the company confirms 40,00,000 fully diluted shares. What percentage of the company does the grant represent? Enter the percentage, for example 1.5 for one and a half percent.
body.explanation: 8,000 ÷ 40,00,000 = 0.002, which is 0.2%. Without the denominator, the option count means nothing, which is exactly why you must ask for it.

body.title: Which Clause Would You Fix First?
body.question: You can negotiate exactly one change to the letter quoted above, at an unlisted company that has never run a buyback. Which change is worth the most to you?
options: A lower exercise price, from ₹25 to ₹10
An exercise window of several years after leaving, instead of 60 days
Quarterly vesting changed to monthly vesting
body.explanation: Dropping the exercise price saves ₹1,20,000 across the whole grant, and 1,000 extra options adds about ₹2,25,000 of paper value. Both are worth less than the window, which decides whether you can keep any of it at all. A 60-day window forces you to fund ₹2,00,000 plus perquisite tax while changing jobs, for shares with no buyer. Many people simply let the options lapse, so the whole grant goes to zero.

children.text: What You Can Actually Negotiate
Employees assume grant terms are fixed. Quantity usually is, because it is benchmarked internally. Several other terms are far more flexible than candidates expect, particularly for senior hires.

body.title: The ask, and how to frame it

columns.label: Worth asking for
points: A longer post-exit exercise window, ideally until a liquidity event
Double trigger acceleration on a change of control
Written confirmation of the fully diluted share count and latest valuation
Inclusion in the next buyback window, if one is planned
A commitment to refresh grants in year two or three

columns.label: Rarely moves
points: The grant quantity, which is usually set by internal bands
The exercise price, which follows scheme rules and the face value floor
The standard vesting length, though the cliff sometimes moves
Anti-dilution protection, which employees essentially never receive
Scheme-wide clauses that apply to every employee equally

children.text: Note the last one on the right.
Anti-dilution protection
is an investor right. Asking for it marks you as unserious, and asking instead for a longer exercise window marks you as someone who has read the document.

markDefs.definition: Protection that adjusts an existing holder’s position when new shares are issued at a lower price. Investors get it. Employees almost never do.

body.text: Frame every request as a problem you are solving for the company, not a concession you want. "A longer window means I will not be forced to sell or lapse, so the cap table stays clean and I stay aligned" lands very differently from "60 days is unfair".

body.title: A short script for the conversation

children.text: "Thank you for the grant. Before I sign, could you share the scheme document and confirm the fully diluted share count and the latest fair market value? I want to understand the grant properly rather than just the number of options."

"One clause I would like to discuss is the 60-day exercise window. Since the company is unlisted, exercising within 60 days of leaving would mean funding both the exercise price and the perquisite tax out of pocket for shares I could not sell. Would the company consider a longer window, or an extension until a liquidity event?"
"If that is not possible within the scheme, is there a company practice of extending windows case by case, and who approves it?"
Ask in writing, keep it factual, and accept a no gracefully. You will still have learned exactly how this company treats its employee shareholders, which is worth knowing before you join.

body.title: The Document That Governs
body.textWithBlank: Where your grant letter and the company’s ESOP ___ document conflict, it is the latter, approved by shareholders, that generally governs.
body.explanation: This is why reading only the grant letter is not enough. Leaver definitions, clawback, amendment rights and change of control treatment usually live in the scheme document.

body.title: The Letter That Arrives on a Friday
body.scenario: Deepa is joining a Series A fintech in Bengaluru as a senior product manager, moving from a listed bank. The offer is ₹26 lakh cash, down from ₹34 lakh, plus 12,000 options at a ₹20 exercise price. The recruiter sends the grant letter on Friday evening and asks her to sign by Monday. The letter does not mention the total share count, the exercise window is 90 days after leaving, and the scheme document has not been shared.
body.prompt: What should she do over the weekend, and what should she send on Monday?
body.modelAnswer: She should not sign blind because of an artificial deadline, and a reasonable company will not withdraw an offer over a two-day delay for legitimate questions. Over the weekend she should work out what she can: she is giving up ₹8 lakh a year of cash, so ₹32 lakh over four years, and she needs the fully diluted share count and the latest valuation to judge whether 12,000 options plausibly covers that. On Monday she should send one short, friendly email asking for the scheme document, the fully diluted share count, the latest fair market value and its date, the company’s buyback history if any, and whether the 90-day window can be extended. She should also ask what the perquisite tax position would look like at the current valuation, since that is the cash she would need on exit. If the answers are clear and the numbers stack up, she signs. If the company refuses to share the scheme document or pressures her further, she has learned something important about how it will treat her as a shareholder.

body.description: A plain-language official summary of how employee stock option plans work, from the regulator itself.

points: Ask for the scheme document, not just the grant letter. The clauses that hurt usually live in the scheme.
A grant of options is meaningless without the fully diluted share count. Convert it to a percentage before you judge it.
The eight clauses worth reading closely are quantity, exercise price, vesting, exit window, leaver definitions, clawback, change of control and amendment rights.
The post-exit exercise window is the single most valuable clause to negotiate at an unlisted company.
Treat the words discretion and clawback as flags wherever they appear.
Quantity and exercise price rarely move, but windows, acceleration, refresh commitments and disclosure often do.
Ask in writing, frame requests as problems solved for the company, and accept a no gracefully while noting what it tells you.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment, tax or legal advice. The sample clause is illustrative and not drawn from any company’s actual document. For a grant that is material to your finances, have the scheme document reviewed by a qualified professional.
